submission.natural_language_explanation: The pole fires on the main clause of a sentence whose opening constituent is a fronted non-subject phrase - a subordinate clause ('Because/When/Although/Since ...'), a prepositional, participial or purpose-infinitive phrase, or a fronted object ('This book, ...') - peaking at the hand-over into that main clause: the comma closing the fronted constituent when one is there (optional, not required), then the main clause's first subject token (a determiner or pronoun such as 'the/its/they/we/I/it/there') and its first verb. It is near zero when the subject comes first in its sentence, when the next clause is merely coordinated with and/but/so, at enumeration commas, and at sentence-initial subjects after a full stop.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The keeper's first duty each evening is to climb the tower before sunset and inspect every part of the lamp. The brass reservoir holds enough oil for fourteen hours of burning, and the keeper measures the level against a marked rod. A dirty chimney, a crooked wick, and a loose mantle each spoil the beam in a different way. The keeper trims the wick with a pair of curved scissors, polishes the lens with a soft cloth, and writes the time in the station ledger. Wind matters more than rain on this coast. A steady gale from the northwest can throw spray forty metres up the tower, and the salt dries on the glass in a pale film. The keeper wipes the panes again after every watch. Fog is worse. A beam shortens to a few hundred metres in thick fog, and the horn then carries the warning instead. The horn runs on compressed air, and its valves need clearing every second week. Summer keeps the tower warm enough for shirtsleeves, and winter frosts the iron stairs so that every climb takes twice as long. Supplies arrive by boat whenever the tide allows, and the keeper counts barrels of oil, sacks of flour, and crates of candles against the manifest. A storm can delay the boat for a month. The keeper then rations the oil, mends the nets, and trades with the fishermen for vegetables and rope. The mainland inspector visits once a year, and he reads the log, tests the lens, and checks the condition of the stairs. A keeper who misses an entry or leaves the glass smeared will hear about it for the rest of the year. The work suits people who like their own company and a fixed routine. Each keeper learns the moods of the sea, the habits of the seabirds, and the hour when the fleet rounds the point. The lamp itself is simple. A circular wick draws oil from the reservoir, a clockwork movement turns the lens, and a chain of weights in the tower column drives the rotation. The keeper winds the weights at the start of every watch and again at the halfway mark. A stopped movement still leaves a burning light, but the beam stops sweeping and the fleet loses its bearing on the rocks. The keeper keeps a hand lantern by the door for the rounds and a barometer in the kitchen for the weather. A falling glass means a blow within the day, and the keeper double-checks the shutters and the oil supply. The station cat earns its keep by keeping the storeroom free of mice. Meals are plain and regular. The keeper eats bread, salted fish, and whatever the garden produces, and drinks tea at every watch. Visitors are rare, and most of them arrive on the supply boat. Although the lamp had been serviced twice that month, Marguerite still carried a lantern on her evening rounds.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Arctic amplification is the name researchers give to the fact that the far north has warmed several times faster than the rest of the planet. The pattern appears in the instrumental record and in ice cores that cover the industrial period. Bright snow and sea ice reflect most of the sunlight that reaches them. Dark open water and dark rock absorb nearly all of it. That difference in reflectivity drives a feedback loop which scientists call the ice-albedo effect. The loop works like this: the ice retreats, the ocean is exposed, the surface gains heat, and the next winter produces thinner ice. Thinner ice melts earlier in spring, and the cycle repeats with more force each decade. The ocean also stores heat through summer and releases it through autumn, and the delay pushes the freeze later. Warm autumn air holds more water vapour, and heavier snow then falls on the surrounding land. Heavy snow insulates the ground, and the soil stays warm enough for microbes to keep respiring. Microbes release carbon dioxide and methane, and both gases trap outgoing heat. Permafrost holds large stores of carbon in frozen plant material. Thawing ground exposes that material to decay, and the release adds to the greenhouse load. Satellites have measured the extent of sea ice since 1979. The September minimum has fallen by roughly a third over that record. The decline varies from year to year, and wind and currents shift the ice around the basin. Scientists at several institutes have compared these measurements against climate models. The models reproduce the overall decline, and most of them still underestimate the speed of the change in the north. Communities in Alaska, Canada, Greenland, Norway, and Russia report thinner ice, later freeze-up, and shorter travel seasons. Hunters depend on stable ice for travel, and a late freeze disrupts the autumn hunt. Thawing permafrost cracks roads, tilts buildings, and weakens pipeline supports. Engineers have answered the problem with insulation, with heat pipes, and with elevated foundations. Snow cover on land has shrunk in spring, and the melt date now arrives about a week earlier than it did in the 1970s. Rivers carry more water in spring and less in late summer, and hydroelectric operators adjust their schedules. Reindeer herders move their animals along routes that their grandparents used, and the routes no longer hold. The changes interact, and each one nudges the others. Scientists continue to argue about the exact share of the warming that the feedbacks explain. The disagreement concerns timing and magnitude rather than direction. Most researchers agree that the trend will continue for decades, and they agree that the consequences reach well beyond the Arctic. Weather patterns in the middle latitudes shift as the north warms, and the shifts affect harvests, water supplies, and heating bills. The subject attracts attention from economists, engineers, and public health specialists, and each group reads the evidence through its own concerns. Data archives grow every year, and the analysis keeps improving. Models run hotter in the north, and observations run hotter still. The core finding is stable: the Arctic warms faster than the rest of the planet, and the feedbacks make the difference.

It is near zero when the subject comes first in its sentence, when the next clause is merely coordinated with and/but/so, at enumeration commas, and at sentence-initial subjects after a full stop.
